Report_ID: Fear of falling (FES-I total score) at T1, post 16-week intervention: intervention vs usual care (group-by-time interaction)
Title: Effects of a complex intervention on fall risk in the general practitioner setting: a cluster randomized controlled trial
Author: Freiberger E, Blank WA, Salb J, Geilhof B, Hentschke C, Landendoerfer P, Halle M, Siegrist M
Comment: No post-intervention FES-I group means or SDs are reported numerically (shown only graphically in Figure 2); only the mixed-model IG−CG estimate (−3.7, SE 0.98, Bonferroni-corrected 95% CI −6.15 to −1.25) and Cohen's d = −0.26 are available. The CI fields were stored in group_1_ci_lower/upper because they belong to the IG−CG difference estimate (M_diff), not to a single arm. test_statistic = −3.7/0.98 = −3.78 computed from the reported coefficient and SE (paper reports only a likelihood-ratio-test P-value). Ns are baseline per-arm Ns (IG 222, CG 156); final analysed per-arm Ns are not reported. Cluster randomized design, but the GP cluster level explained negligible variance and was dropped, so estimates come from a two-level model. Negative values favour the intervention (less fear of falling); the plan's sign convention (positive Hedges' g favours intervention) requires reversing the sign of this reported d.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Intervention group (IG): 16-week complex exercise intervention with behavioural/cognitive components') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Study Environment: GP office setting / community-based group exercise sessions
Content length: 16-week intervention (16 supervised weekly 60-min group sessions plus ≥1 unsupervised home session/week from week 5)
Participant type: functionally declined, community-dwelling older persons aged 65+ at high risk of falling, recruited via general practitioners (mean age 78.1 years, SD 5.9; 75.4% female)
Outcome measurement: Mixed-model (random intercept, random slope) estimate of the difference in change between IG and CG on FES-I total score
Outcome variable: Fear of falling (FES-I total score) at T1, post 16-week intervention: intervention vs usual care (group-by-time interaction)
effect_direction: favours intervention (FES-I reduced by 3.7 points in IG relative to CG; reported d = -0.26, i.e. less fear with intervention)

Report_ID: Fear of falling at Time 2 (12 months) — cognitive-behavioral vs discussion control
Title: Attempts to Prevent Falls and Injury: A Prospective Community Study
Author: Reinsch, MacRae, Lachenbruch, & Tobis
Comment: Cluster-randomised by senior center but analysed at individual level (clustering ignored by the paper; no design effect reported). Secondary outcomes assessed only in the subsample present at both Time 1 and Time 2 (n = 112 overall). The discussion control group (n = 23) is shared with the exercise-cognitive comparison; per the synthesis plan its n should be halved (≈11.5) when both comparisons are pooled — the raw reported n = 23 is recorded here. No inferential statistic specific to fear of falling reported; paper states only non-significance. M_diff not computed because this is a 4-arm trial, not a simple two-group design.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Cognitive-behavioral intervention (1-hr class, 1 day/week for 1 year: safety curriculum, relaxation training, videogame playing)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Participant type: community-dwelling adults over age 60 recruited from 16 senior centers
Recruitment source: 16 senior centers in Orange County (n = 134) and Los Angeles County (n = 96), California
Outcome variable: Fear of falling at Time 2 (12 months) — cognitive-behavioral vs discussion control
additional_group_ns: Arms reported but not used for this comparison: Exercise-only n = 37 at Time 2 (excluded as exercise-only, no CBT component); Exercise-cognitive n = 50 at Time 2 (extracted as a separate row/comparison)
effect_direction: slightly favours intervention (CBT 1.6 vs discussion control 1.7; higher = more worry), non-significant

Report_ID: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (FES total score) at 2 months — CB + Tai Chi vs control
Title: Reducing the fear of falling among community-dwelling elderly adults through cognitive-behavioural strategies and intense Tai Chi exercise: a randomized controlled trial
Author: Huang, Yang & Liu
Comment: F = 4.09 is the omnibus one-way ANOVA across all three groups at 2 months (df not reported); p recorded as the table footnote threshold *P < 0.05. Post hoc indicated group 3 (CB + Tai Chi) > group 1 (control). FES is a confidence scale (higher = less fear), so sign must be reversed per the synthesis plan. Control group n = 61 is the 2-month n and is shared with the CB-alone comparison row.; N-INCONSISTENCY: n_control(61) + n_treatment(56) = 117 ≠ n_total(186) — verify per-group Ns
Recruitment source: Randomly selected registered households in a rural community, Yi-Lan county, north-eastern Taiwan
Outcome measurement: Mean (SD) FES total score at 2-month assessment per group
Outcome variable: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (FES total score) at 2 months — CB + Tai Chi vs control
additional_group_ns: CB alone arm (not included in this row): n = 60 at 2 months, FES mean 90.13 (SD 16.85) — recorded as a separate row
effect_direction: favours intervention (CB + Tai Chi FES 96.71 vs control 88.69; higher confidence = less fear, so sign reversal gives advantage to intervention)

Title: Testing the Senior Exercise Self-efficacy Project (SESEP) for Use with Urban Dwelling Minority Older Adults
Author: Resnick, Luisi, & Vogel
Comment: Table 3 reports baseline and follow-up means/SDs but no per-row Ns; group Ns taken from the Results text ("Follow-up testing included 103 participants (62%), 39 from control sites and 64 from treatment sites"). Trial was cluster-randomized (6 vs 7 senior centers) but analysed at the individual level with no clustering correction by the authors; no cluster-adjusted estimate is reported, so sample sizes here are unadjusted. Fear of falling is a secondary outcome measured by a single 0-4 item, not FES-I. M_diff/effect size not computed as the analysis was a MANOVA and no effect size was reported ("NA" in Table 3).; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('SESEP intervention (exercise + efficacy-enhancing/behaviour-change component)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Participant type: Community-dwelling minority older adults aged 60+ attending senior centers in NYC public housing
Recruitment source: Free 1-day heart health screening events at 13 participating senior centers in NYC public housing developments
Outcome measurement: Self-reported single-item fear of falling, 0-4; higher = more fear
effect_direction: slightly favours intervention (SESEP 1.6 vs attention control 1.8; higher = more fear), non-significant (F = 1.9, p = .17)
outcome_units: points on 0-4 fear of falling rating

Report_ID: Fear of falling (falls-related self-efficacy/confidence) at 6 months (end of intervention)
Title: A Randomized Trial of a Multicomponent Home Intervention to Reduce Functional Difficulties in Older Adults
Author: Gitlin, Winter, Dennis, Corcoran, Schinfeld, Hauck
Comment: Group means ± SD at 6 months are UNADJUSTED observed values; the M_diff of 0.61 (P=.001) is the ANCOVA-ADJUSTED mean difference (adjusted for baseline value, race, living arrangement, functional difficulty, depressive symptoms) and is not equal to the raw difference (7.79-7.45=0.34). The paper's 95% CI is internally inconsistent: Table 2 reports 0.15-0.97 while the Abstract reports 0.26-0.96 for the same effect; SE_diff therefore not derived from the CI. Per-group 6-month Ns (154/146) are from the Results text, not from Table 2 cells. Higher score = LESS fear (confidence scale), so sign reversal is needed per the synthesis plan. Intervention is multicomponent OT/PT with cognitive-behavioural strategy components rather than formal CBT.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Experimental (multicomponent OT/PT home intervention)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Participant type: Community-living adults aged 70 and older, cognitively intact (MMSE >23), not receiving home care, reporting difficulty with one or more ADLs or two IADLs
Recruitment source: Area agency on aging, media announcements, posters at senior housing and community settings (Philadelphia)
Outcome measurement: Mean response across 13 items (Falls Efficacy Scale + 3 ABC items), 1.00-10.00, higher = less fear; observed 6-month group means ± SD and ANCOVA-adjusted mean difference (adjusted for baseline value, race, living arrangement, functional difficulty, depressive symptoms)
Outcome variable: Fear of falling (falls-related self-efficacy/confidence) at 6 months (end of intervention)
effect_direction: favours intervention (7.79 vs 7.45 on a confidence index where higher = less fear; adjusted mean difference 0.61, p = .001)

Report_ID: Fear of falling (concerns about falling, 14-item scale) at 2-month follow-up (immediately post-intervention)
Title: Effects of a Multicomponent Cognitive Behavioral Group Intervention on Fear of Falling and Activity Avoidance in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial
Author: Zijlstra et al.
Comment: Means/SDs in Table 3 are crude (unadjusted); the mean difference -1.51 is adjusted for baseline values and covariates. Per-group analysed Ns at 2 months are NOT reported in the table; group_1_n/group_2_n are the randomized group sizes verbatim from Results ("260 were randomly assigned to the control group and 280 to the intervention group") and therefore overstate the analysed sample (135 participants were lost to follow-up overall). SE_diff was derived from the reported 95% CI as (−0.20 − (−2.81))/3.92 = 0.666; it was not reported directly.
Participant type: community-dwelling adults aged 70 and older reporting fear of falling and fear-induced activity avoidance
Recruitment source: random samples of 7,431 community-dwelling older adults from municipal registry offices in two Dutch communities
Outcome measurement: Crude post-intervention mean ± SD per group; adjusted mixed-effects linear regression mean difference (95% CI), p-value and effect size
Outcome variable: Fear of falling (concerns about falling, 14-item scale) at 2-month follow-up (immediately post-intervention)
effect_direction: favours intervention (25.5 vs 28.2; higher = more concern; adjusted mean difference -1.51, p = .02)

Report_ID: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (balance confidence, ABC Scale) at 6 months (first post-intervention assessment)
Title: Long-Term Effects of Three Multicomponent Exercise Interventions on Physical Performance and Fall-Related Psychological Outcomes in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Author: Freiberger E, Häberle L, Spirduso WW, Zijlstra GAR
Comment: ABC is a confidence-type scale (higher = more confidence/less fear), so the sign must be reversed per the synthesis plan before computing the SMD. Balance confidence was assessed at follow-up only (no baseline), so no change scores exist; the 6-month assessment is the earliest available post-intervention timepoint (intervention lasted 16 weeks). Table 4 mean difference is coded CG minus Multifaceted Group and is adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, living situation, education, fear of falling and having fallen in the past 6 months. SE_diff was not reported; derived as (0.78 - (-11.25))/3.92 = 3.069 from the reported 95% CI. Per-timepoint analysed Ns from Table 3 were used rather than randomised Ns (CG 80, MG 73). No p-value was reported for this comparison.
Study Environment: community (group sessions at the Institute of Sport Science)
Participant type: community-dwelling older adults aged 70-90 who had fallen in the past 6 months or reported fear of falling
Recruitment source: Health insurance company membership database, Erlangen, Germany
Outcome measurement: Post-intervention mean ± SD per arm (crude results, Table 3) and adjusted mixed-effects mean difference CG minus Multifaceted Group with 95% CI (Table 4)
Outcome variable: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (balance confidence, ABC Scale) at 6 months (first post-intervention assessment)
additional_group_ns: Excluded exercise-only arms at 6 months (no cognitive-behavioural component): Strength and Balance Group n=56, mean 145.8 ± 18.1; Fitness Group n=57, mean 148.6 ± 16.8
follow_up_timepoint: intermediate follow-up (>1 to 6 months after intervention end)
effect_direction: favours control (MG ABC 142.7 vs CG 150.3; higher confidence = less fear, so the multifaceted arm had more fear), non-significant

Report_ID: Fear of falling (FES-I) at week 8, immediately post-intervention
Title: Integrated Exposure Therapy and Exercise Reduces Fear of Falling and Avoidance in Older Adults: A Randomized Pilot Study
Author: Wetherell JL, Bower ES, Johnson K, Chang DG, Ward SR, Petkus AJ
Comment: Post-intervention (week 8) FES-I means and SDs are NOT reported numerically anywhere in the text or tables (shown only graphically in Figure 2 with standard-error bars), so group means/SDs were left empty; only the reported F statistic, p value and Cohen's d could be extracted. The Results text reports d = -1.23 (negative = less fear in ABLE, i.e. favours intervention), whereas the Abstract and Conclusions report the same effect as d = 1.23; the value is recorded verbatim from the Results. The d comes from a covariate-adjusted (credibility, psychiatric disorder) repeated-measures mixed model, not from raw means. Baseline FES-I (Table 2: FPE 39.0 (6.8), ABLE 40.7 (7.3)) is baseline only and was not used as a post-intervention value.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('ABLE (integrated exposure therapy, cognitive restructuring, Otago exercise, home safety evaluation)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Publication Status: accepted manuscript (The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry)
Participant type: community-dwelling older adults aged 65-91 (M=77.9, SD=7.3) with disproportionate fear of falling (FES-I > 27, low-to-moderate objective fall risk)
Recruitment source: senior health fairs, community presentations, referrals from geriatric care providers
Outcome measurement: Falls Efficacy Scale-International total score at week 8 (in-home assessment by blinded research associate)
Outcome variable: Fear of falling (FES-I) at week 8, immediately post-intervention
effect_direction: favours intervention (ABLE showed significantly lower FES-I than education control at week 8; F(1,37) = 5.57, p = .02, Cohen's d = -1.23)

Report_ID: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (FES(S)) at 12 weeks
Title: Fall Preventive Exercise With or Without Behavior Change Support for Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial With Short-Term Follow-up
Author: Arkkukangas, Söderlund, Eriksson, Johansson
Comment: Three-arm trial; the paper reports only an omnibus one-way ANOVA F(2,158)=1.10, P=.35 across all three arms — no pairwise OEP+MI vs control test statistic is reported. Group means, SDs and Ns for the two plan-relevant arms were taken directly from Table 2. M_diff/SE_diff not computed because the reported analysis is a three-group omnibus ANOVA rather than a simple two-group comparison. FES(S) is a confidence-type scale (higher = less fear), so the sign must be reversed downstream per the synthesis plan. Full control n (55) used because only one eligible intervention arm shares it.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('OEP + motivational interviewing (OEP + MI)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False); N-INCONSISTENCY (multi-group): sum of additional_group_ns = 54 ≠ n_total(161) — verify all group Ns
Study Environment: Participants' own homes or health care centres
Topic of Content: Home-based strength/balance exercise (Otago Exercise Program) with motivational interviewing behaviour change support
Participant type: Community-dwelling older adults aged 75+ (mean age 83 years) using walking aids or home care
Recruitment source: Health centres and municipal home care services in 3 communities in central Sweden, recruited by care managers, occupational therapists and physiotherapists
Outcome measurement: Post-intervention (12-week) mean and SD per arm, intention-to-treat (Table 2)
Outcome variable: Fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy (FES(S)) at 12 weeks
additional_group_ns: Third arm not used for this comparison (exercise-only, no behaviour-change component): OEP alone, n = 54 at 12 weeks, FES(S) 12 wk mean 103.8 (SD 22.1); baseline 103.3 (21.3)
effect_direction: slightly favours intervention (OEP + MI 109.5 vs control 106.2; higher self-efficacy = less fear), between-group difference non-significant

Report_ID: Concerns about falls (fear of falling), FES-I total score at 5-month follow-up
Title: Effectiveness of a home-based cognitive behavioral program to manage concerns about falls in community-dwelling, frail older people: results of a randomized controlled trial
Author: Dorresteijn et al.
Comment: p-value recorded as 0.001 because the paper states "< .001" (one-tailed test). The 95% CI is one-sided (lower bound = -infinity), so only the upper bound (-2.15) is recorded and SE_diff cannot be derived from the CI width. The adjusted mean difference is covariate-adjusted (baseline score, level of concerns about falls, age, gender, perceived general health, falls in past 6 months); the raw group means/SDs are unadjusted. Ns are the analysed (not randomised) samples; randomised Ns were 195 control / 194 intervention.
domain: geriatrics / falls prevention / fear of falling
Participant type: Community-dwelling frail older people aged 70 years and older with fair/poor perceived health, concerns about falls and related activity avoidance
Recruitment source: Random address samples drawn from three municipal registry offices in the south of the Netherlands
Outcome measurement: Mean (SD) FES-I total score per group plus adjusted mean difference from mixed-effects linear regression (intention-to-treat)
Outcome variable: Concerns about falls (fear of falling), FES-I total score at 5-month follow-up
follow_up_timepoint: intermediate follow-up (>1 to 6 months after intervention end)
effect_direction: favours intervention (FES-I 31.73 vs 35.30; adjusted mean difference -3.53, p < .001, d = 0.34)
